messages.subject: Sampling from inverted beta/dirichlet
parts:
Hey everyone,

I'm fitting a fairly weird model (one that I've posted here in the past) that contains mixtures.

Because I want to favor categorization, I prefer sampling mixture weights (per case) from, e.g., a beta or dirichlet where the parameters are < 1. That puts more probability over 0s and 1s, and helps 'encourage' assignment to one cluster over others.

However, I noticed today that when using beta(.2,.2) as a prior, for example, that sampling was *slow* (like, 45 minutes later, and only hitting 10%, slow), and I assume that it's because so MUCH probability is over 0 and 1, and the geometry of that is awful to sample from (the negative log of that would be like an inverted U, constrained at 0 and 1).

Because of that, is it preferred to instead parameterize as log-odds and sample from a wide logistic?

That is, is it preferred to use:
vector[N] pi_logit;
pi_logit ~ logistic(pi_logit_mean, 5); pi_logit_mean ~ logistic(0,5);

as opposed to:
vector[N] pi;
pi ~ dbeta(alpha*scale,beta*scale); alpha = (pi_mean); beta = 1 - pi_mean; scale = .2; pi_mean ~ uniform(0,1)

I assume the logistic is easier to sample from, geometrically, than a beta/dirichlet that is highly pointed near bounded areas (0 and 1). Am I correct in thinking about this?

Hi Stephen,

It's actually very hard to follow without the full model. I'd suggest posting a simple example with the full Stan program if you want specific help. 

Questions:
- why not simplex type for pi?

- does it work with simulated data?

Regarding geometry: one thing that comes up often is that at first glance you might think that the geometry is determined by the parameters and the model, without data. The data + model together determine the shape of the joint probability distribution function as a function of the pareters. That's why we have this centered vs non-centered parameterization. It's the data in combination with the model that makes the geometry work or not. (I'm sure there are models where no matter what data is provided it won't work.) If you want to start talking about the geometry in depth, you'll have to not only provide the program, but also some data.

Hopefully you're able to provide a working Stan program or two (or three?) and then someone can help with your program. Without them, everything's a wild guess.


Daniel

On Sep 30, 2016, at 6:00 AM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:

I understand that stan samples from the joint posterior.

I'm simply stating that my priors are purposefully placing greater probability toward constrained areas to encourage clustering (encouraging probability values of 0 and 1), which likely causes the posterior to be difficult to sample from, as the -log of that creates an extremely steep "hill" of sorts. To avoid that, I can reparameterize in terms of logits (which aren't constrained), and use a prior that is fairly wide so that larger logit values are more probable.
Extending that to a multigroup case is the difficulty. beta -> dirichlet, as logit -> ?; I'm thinking I could use a MVN approximation to a 'multivariate logistic' distribution of sorts.

messages.subject: Re: Sampling from inverted beta/dirichlet
parts:
Alright. Here is the code:

data {
    int N;
    vector[N] x;
    int K;
    real dirichlet_scale;
}
parameters{
    ordered[K] means;
    vector<lower=0>[K] sds;
//    simplex[K] pi[N];
    vector<lower=0>[K] pi_logit[N];
    vector<lower=0>[K] beta0;
}
transformed parameters{
    simplex[K] pi_mean;
    simplex[K] pi[N];
    pi_mean = softmax(beta0);
    for(n in 1:N){
        pi[n] = softmax(pi_logit[n]);
    }
}
model{
    vector[K] lp_nk[N];
    vector[N] lp_n;
   
    means ~ normal(0,4);
    sds ~ cauchy(0,3);
    beta0 ~ logistic(0,1);
    for(n in 1:N){
        for(k in 1:K){
            pi_logit[n,k] ~ logistic(beta0[k],3);
        }
//        pi[n] ~ dirichlet(pi_mean*dirichlet_scale);
    }
   
    for(n in 1:N){
        for(k in 1:K){
            lp_nk[n,k] = log(pi[n,k]) + normal_lpdf(x[n] | means[k], sds[k]);
        }
        lp_n[n] = log_sum_exp(lp_nk[n]);
    }
target += sum(lp_n);
}

The goal of the model (in this toy example) is to fit a mixture model, but with the ability to predict latent class memberships.
In this particular case, it's an intercept-only model, so each person's "predicted membership" is given by beta0.

You can use softmax regression to predict logits; I use priors to constrain the intercepts to be positive and logistic-distributed, because softmax regression needs some constraining (several equal solutions otherwise).
In the dirichlet method, the logits are transformed to probabilities, and each individual's latent membership probabilities (pi) is assumed to be dirichlet-distributed with the predicted probabilities as the hyperparameter; the scale forces probability to be allocated toward 0s and 1s, and so encourages loading on one cluster. The geometry, however, is extremely weird, because it creates a very steep inverted-U that causes difficulty sampling and divergent transitions (to see what it could do, look in R at curve(dbeta(x,.4*.2,.6*.2,log=TRUE)*-1,0,1) ). I'm guessing the posterior has a ton of probability right at the bounded regions and it's creating difficulties.

Another method keeps using logits.
An individual's logits are assumed to be multivariate-logistic distributed with mean-logits at the predicted logits; because the assumed multi-variate-logistic has no covariance, it's the same as using univariate logistics each with a beta0 mean. To again encourage high probabilities for certain clusters, we let the scale be large (and so one can easily have very high logits).
Using this method, no divergent transitions occur, and the model works.

So it seems like I may have answered my own question --- Sampling from inverted-betas and inverted-dirichlets makes the posterior geometry difficult to sample from, it's slow and causes divergent transitions. Using an alternative method that uses only logit-sampling works fine, and it seems to be because the geometry is more forgiving.
On Thursday, September 29, 2016 at 10:33:14 PM UTC-5, Stephen Martin wrote:

Hey everyone,

I'm fitting a fairly weird model (one that I've posted here in the past) that contains mixtures.

Because I want to favor categorization, I prefer sampling mixture weights (per case) from, e.g., a beta or dirichlet where the parameters are < 1. That puts more probability over 0s and 1s, and helps 'encourage' assignment to one cluster over others.

However, I noticed today that when using beta(.2,.2) as a prior, for example, that sampling was *slow* (like, 45 minutes later, and only hitting 10%, slow), and I assume that it's because so MUCH probability is over 0 and 1, and the geometry of that is awful to sample from (the negative log of that would be like an inverted U, constrained at 0 and 1).

Because of that, is it preferred to instead parameterize as log-odds and sample from a wide logistic?

That is, is it preferred to use:

as opposed to:
vector[N] pi;

I assume the logistic is easier to sample from, geometrically, than a beta/dirichlet that is highly pointed near bounded areas (0 and 1). Am I correct in thinking about this?

parts:
For the sake of posterity, here's my [really messy] implementation of multinomial latent class regression:
Two weirds thing in this is that: using a logistic(0,1) vs a logistic(0,3) for softmax really shouldn't make a difference, since it's all relative. However, using 3 seems to still favor high-probability categorization.
Second, Rather than defining one's latent membership probability as a linear function, I still say it's "predicted" from a linear function with a standard error of 1 logit. Either way works, but allowing individuals to differ from the line can improve clustering accuracy (because it permits two individuals with the same betas and predictors to differ). Too large an error (e.g., 5 standard deviations), and the predictors are meaningless and contribute nothing to clustering. So if you want high accuracy clustering and also to estimate how predictors relate to cluster-membership, it seems like setting an sd=1 is reasonable.

data {
    int N;
    int J;
    int K;
    vector[N] x;
    matrix[N,J] predictor;

}
parameters{
    ordered[K] means;
    vector<lower=0>[K] sds;

vector<lower=0>[K] pi_logit[N];
    vector<lower=0>[K] beta0;

matrix[J,K] beta;
}
transformed parameters{
    simplex[K] pi[N];
//    vector[K] pi_logit[N];

for(n in 1:N){
        pi[n] = softmax(pi_logit[n]);
    }
}
model{
    vector[K] lp_nk[N];
    vector[N] lp_n;
   
    means ~ normal(0,4);
    sds ~ cauchy(0,3);

beta0 ~ logistic(0,3);
    for(k in 1:K){
        beta[1:J,k] ~ logistic(0,3);

}
    for(n in 1:N){
        for(k in 1:K){
pi_logit[n,k] ~ logistic(beta0[k] + predictor[n]*beta[1:J,k],1);

}
    }
   
    for(n in 1:N){
        for(k in 1:K){
            lp_nk[n,k] = log(pi[n,k]) + normal_lpdf(x[n] | means[k], sds[k]);
        }
        lp_n[n] = log_sum_exp(lp_nk[n]);
    }
target += sum(lp_n);
}

This latter model suffers from div. transitions and incorrect parameter estimates.

No idea why, and I welcome any input about that.

However, I noticed today that when using beta(.2,.2) as a prior, for example, that sampling was *slow* (like, 45 minutes later, and only hitting 10%, slow), and I assume that it's because so MUCH probability is over 0 and 1, and the geometry of that is awful to sample from (the negative log of that would be like an inverted U, constrained at 0 and 1).

Because of that, is it preferred to instead parameterize as log-odds and sample from a wide logistic?

That is, is it preferred to use:
vector[N] pi_logit;
pi_logit ~ logistic(pi_logit_mean, 5); pi_logit_mean ~ logistic(0,5);

as opposed to:
vector[N] pi;
pi ~ dbeta(alpha*scale,beta*scale); alpha = (pi_mean); beta = 1 - pi_mean; scale = .2; pi_mean ~ uniform(0,1)

I assume the logistic is easier to sample from, geometrically, than a beta/dirichlet that is highly pointed near bounded areas (0 and 1). Am I correct in thinking about this?

As per Bob's suggestion, I constrained beta0[1] (arbitrarily) to 0, so that the logits have some sort of scale. I then allowed the beta0[2:K] to be negative or positive (rather than constrained to be positive).
This led to divergent transitions and very wrong, albeit consistent estimates of beta0[2:K] and the latent class means/sds.

Honestly, I have NO idea why that would be the case.

To clarify (and review):
One model uses softmax regression, but constrains the intercept-logits (beta0) to be positive and ~logistic(0,3); with this parametization, several combinations of beta0s are possible, but it does not affect the model because once softmax'd, the probabilities are the same.
The other model uses softmax, but constrains beta0[1] to be 0; the others are ~ logistic(0,3) with no constraint. This should yield the same model as above (intuitively, to me, anyway), but sets a scale for which other logits to be compared to (no more multiple combinations of beta0s should be possible). This latter model suffers from div. transitions and incorrect parameter estimates.

No idea why, and I welcome any input about that.
